newsitem.title: FRANCE: French unions, government debate work flexibility.
newsitem.headline: French unions, government debate work flexibility.

text.p: A French trade union leader said on Thursday he had asked President Jacques Chirac for clarification about a proposed youth job training scheme which looked like a bid to revive a sub-minimum wage for the young.

The challenge coincided with the opening of consultations with trade unions by Labour Minister Jacques Barrot on the issue of greater flexibility in the labour market to combat record 12.7 percent unemployment.

Marc Blondel, general-secretary of the Force Ouvriere union, said he asked Chirac on Thursday about a plan by employers for work training leading to a diploma in exchange for 1,500 francs ($283) a month, just one-quarter of the minimum wage.

He compared the scheme, touted by Chirac last month as a key initiative to combat one-in-four youth unemployment, to a failed bid by ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur in 1994 to introduce a lower minimum wage for young people on work experience, known as the CIP, which was scrapped after huge student protests.

"We need to know whether this is to be training or a work contract," Blondel said of the latest scheme. "These things are not spelled out and I think this is an operation comparable with what they did with the CIP."

The CNPF employers' federation has launched a campaign for greater flexibility, saying industrialists would be more willing to create jobs if it was easier to shed staff in times of economic difficulty.
However trade unions say more than half of all jobs created in France last year were on short-term contracts of a average three-month duration.
"Flexibility" has become a bogey word for French unions, which associate it with what they view as harsh U.S. and British hiring and firing practices.
"Flexibility already exists and there can be no question of getting rid of the court vetting of redundancy plans," white-collar CGC union leader Marc Vilbenoit said after meeting Barrot.
